name: Scalp cooling cap

lead: A scalp cooling cap lowers scalp temperature during chemotherapy so more of your hair is kept through treatment. It comes as frozen gel caps or machine-cooled systems.

Cooling is thought to reduce blood flow and drug exposure at the follicle and slow follicle activity while chemotherapy circulates. It has been evaluated mostly in women with breast cancer, including a randomized trial and cohort study published in JAMA in 2017, plus registries and systematic reviews.

paras: Gel or ice caps are frozen beforehand and swapped during the infusion, while machine systems keep coolant circulating through the cap from a control unit. It is used around chemotherapy sessions, particularly with taxane or anthracycline regimens. It preserves existing hair rather than growing new hair.

Side effects are generally minor. Caps are not advised where cancer is in the scalp skin or in lymphoma or leukemia, and a meta-analysis has examined scalp metastasis risk. US costs are roughly $1,500 to $3,000 per course.

angle.text: Chemotherapy patients wear scalp cooling caps to keep more of their hair through treatment: the chilled scalp reduces how much drug reaches the follicles. It has been studied in trials, mainly in breast cancer patients, and preserves existing hair rather than boosting growth.

lead: A scalp cooling cap is a tight-fitting cap that lowers scalp temperature around chemotherapy sessions so that more of a patient's own hair stays in place. Caps are either manual gel or ice caps that are frozen beforehand and swapped at intervals during treatment, or machine-based systems in which a control unit keeps coolant circulating [1]. The terms cold cap, hypothermia cap and scalp cooling are used interchangeably [1].

The appearance payoff is direct for the people who use it: keeping some or most of the hair through a course of chemotherapy means looking less visibly 'in treatment', needing a wig or head cover less often, and starting regrowth from a fuller base. A 2025 meta-analysis notes that chemotherapy-induced alopecia affects about 65% of patients receiving chemotherapy and harms quality of life [2]. The topic sits at the edge of looksmaxxing, which is mostly about hair loss from androgenetic alopecia, but it is a well-studied example of preserving existing hair [3][4].

Randomized and prospective studies in women receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer have measured how many keep more than half of their hair [3][4][5], and systematic reviews have pooled the wider literature [6][7][2]. Wikipedia notes the approach is likely to be useful with taxane or anthracycline regimens, that caps are not advised where cancer is present in the scalp skin or in lymphoma or leukemia, and that US costs are roughly $1,500 to $3,000 per course [1].

paras: Caps are usually made of neoprene, silicone or polyurethane and filled with gel or ice. Manual caps are frozen to roughly -25 to -30 degrees C before use, while machine systems use a control unit to keep the cap cold [1]. Wikipedia names three major providers of scalp cooling systems, Dignitana, Paxman and Penguin Cold Cap [1].

In manual cold-cap programmes the cap is changed at set intervals, and a helper known in patient communities as a 'capper' often does the swapping. A 2019 nursing case report describes a 23-year-old patient whose mother changed dry-ice caps about every 20 minutes during infusions, with the cap applied before the infusion and worn for 90 minutes afterwards; the patient estimated she lost about 5% of her hair over six cycles. [8] Machine systems avoid the swapping by circulating liquid coolant through the cap. [1]

The first US patent, filed in 1979 and granted in 1984, covered Mark Barron's Chemo Cap, which used frozen gel-filled nylon pouches worn for 15 to 20 minutes before treatment. Studies from the 1980s and early 1990s were discouraging, and the patent expired in 1998 [1].

Research in the 1990s and 2000s reported better results with specific regimens. A 1997 trial of a cold cap in 98 patients on docetaxel judged 86% a success (WHO grade 2 or lower and no wig) [9]. A 2000 study of the Penguin Cold Cap system in 70 patients reported 81% protection overall among those evaluable, with 88% adequate protection for taxane regimens but 36% for a taxane plus anthracycline group [10]. A review of 53 publications covered efficacy, side effects and controversies [6], and an analysis cited by Wikipedia of studies from 1995 to 2003 gave an average success rate of 73% [1].

Controlled evidence grew in the 2010s. A Dutch registry reported outcomes in 1,411 chemotherapy patients [11], and two papers published in JAMA in 2017 reported a randomized trial and a prospective cohort of a scalp cooling device in women with breast cancer [3][4]. The 2025 meta-analysis states that scalp cooling is the only FDA-cleared intervention for chemotherapy-induced alopecia [2].

Cooling the scalp is thought to constrict blood vessels and reduce how much chemotherapy drug reaches hair follicles, and to lower follicle metabolic activity. Reviews of the pathobiology describe chemotherapy-induced alopecia as typically acute diffuse hair loss (dystrophic anagen effluvium) with incidence and severity that vary with the chemotherapy protocol [12]. The 2000 Penguin study kept scalp temperature below 15 degrees C before, during and after chemotherapy by frequent cap changes. [10]

Reported success varies with the chemotherapy regimen and other factors. A study of influencing factors examined characteristics associated with how well scalp cooling works [13], and a systematic review and meta-analysis assessed interventions for preventing chemotherapy-induced alopecia [7]. A systematic review of nonpharmacologic strategies for common chemotherapy adverse effects also addressed the topic [14].

In the SCALP randomized trial at seven US sites, stopped early after an interim analysis, 48 of 95 evaluable women using the cooling device (50.5%) kept more than half of their hair, compared with none of 47 controls.[3] In the companion prospective cohort of 122 women at five centers, 67 of 101 evaluable cooling patients (66.3%) had 50% or less hair loss, against none of 16 controls.[4]

The COOLHAIR randomized trial in 79 patients receiving anthracycline- and/or taxane-based early breast cancer chemotherapy reported hair preservation (50% or less loss) in 39.3% of the cooling arm versus 0% of the observation arm, with less wig or scarf use outside the home before cycle 3 (40.7% versus 95.5%). [5] A meta-analysis of 8 randomized and 9 controlled trials with 1,098 participants reported a relative risk of alopecia of 0.38 with scalp cooling [7]. The Dutch registry of 1,411 patients found outcomes depended heavily on regimen, with satisfaction around 8% after one anthracycline-taxane combination (TAC) and up to 95% after paclitaxel; about half of patients did not wear a head cover at their last session.[11]

Wikipedia describes side effects in chemotherapy patients as generally minor and says caps should not be used when cancer is present in scalp skin, or in people with lymphoma or leukemia [1]. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether scalp cooling during adjuvant or neoadjuvant breast cancer chemotherapy affects the risk of scalp metastases [15].

A 2025 meta-analysis of 67 studies found the most common adverse effects were generalized chills (42%), cap heaviness (35%) and headache (30%); the discontinuation rate was 18%, most often because of progressive alopecia, and scalp metastasis incidence was estimated at 0.15%. [2] In the SCALP trial there were 54 device-related adverse events in the cooling group, all grade 1 or 2, and no serious adverse device events.[3] In the cohort study, 3.8% of patients had mild headache and 2.8% stopped because they felt cold.[4]

Hair loss during chemotherapy is among the most visible effects of treatment, and many patients describe it as altering how they look and are seen by others; a 2019 account in the oncology nursing literature describes a patient who valued her hair and researched cold caps herself. [8] Scalp cooling is a way of keeping some or most of the existing hair through treatment, so that regrowth begins from a fuller starting point.[1]

Reports consistently say results depend on the drug regimen, and the factors influencing effectiveness have been examined in their own study.[13] Registered trials are examining scalp cooling for patients of color and other groups. [16] Wikipedia lists US costs of about $1,500 to $3,000 per course. [1]

Hypothermia caps are also used in other medical contexts. Wikipedia describes induced cooling for newborns with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy and cold wraps for migraine. [1] Within hair-loss culture, scalp cooling differs from drugs such as minoxidil or finasteride because it is used only around chemotherapy sessions for hair loss caused by the treatment. [12]

The SCALP randomized clinical trial and a companion prospective cohort study, both published in JAMA in 2017, assessed a scalp cooling device in women receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer and monitored adverse effects and quality of life [3][4]. COOLHAIR randomized 79 patients [5], the Dutch Scalp Cooling Registry described outcomes in 1,411 patients [11], and systematic reviews and meta-analyses have pooled results on hair preservation, adverse effects and scalp metastasis [7][15][2].

Registered trials include a comparison of a scalp cooling system with a chemical cold cap in primary breast cancer (COHAIR) [17] and a small study of chemotherapy alopecia reduction in breast cancer [18].
